paragraphs.title: Lament over Israel’s Fall and the Call to Seek the Lord

easy.explanation: Amos says he takes up a lamentation against Israel.
easy.q: What does Amos take up against the house of Israel?

answers: She is fallen and has none to raise her up
easy.explanation: The KJV says, “The virgin of Israel is fallen; she shall no more rise.”
easy.q: What happens to the virgin of Israel?

easy.explanation: The Lord says, “Seek ye me, and ye shall live.”
easy.q: What does the Lord command the house of Israel to do?

answers: Only a small remnant will remain
medium.explanation: A city of a thousand will leave a hundred, and one of a hundred will leave ten.
medium.q: What do the numbers in the city illustration show?

medium.explanation: Amos specifically names Bethel, Gilgal, and Beer-sheba.
medium.q: Which places does Amos tell Israel not to seek?

answers: A song or expression of mourning
medium.explanation: A lamentation is an expression of grief over disaster or loss.
medium.q: What does “a lamentation” mean in this passage?

answers: Destruction is set beside a call to seek the Lord and live
The people are told to seek the worship centers
challenge.explanation: Although Amos announces destruction, he calls the people to seek the Lord as the way of life.
challenge.q: What contrast is central to this passage?

answers: He redirects the people from those places to the Lord himself
He promises that all three places will be spared
He describes the borders of Israel
challenge.explanation: The warning not to seek these places emphasizes seeking the Lord instead.
challenge.q: Why does Amos name Bethel, Gilgal, and Beer-sheba?

answers: A movement from judgment toward a possible way of life
A movement from war toward trade
A movement from worship of the Lord toward idols
challenge.explanation: The passage moves from lament and destruction to a call that offers life through seeking the Lord.
challenge.q: What is suggested by the movement from Israel’s fall to “Seek ye me, and ye shall live”?

paragraphs.title: Social Injustice and the Power of the Lord

easy.explanation: The people turn judgment into wormwood.
easy.q: What do the people turn into wormwood?

easy.explanation: The KJV says, “They hate him that rebuketh in the gate.”
easy.q: Whom do they hate in the gate?

easy.explanation: They tread upon the poor and turn aside the poor in the gate.

answers: They will enjoy their houses and vineyards
They will not dwell in their houses or drink their wine
The poor will willingly leave the land
medium.explanation: Those who built houses and planted vineyards will not enjoy them.
medium.q: What will happen to those who exploit the poor?

answers: The Lord can empower the oppressed against the strong
The people divide their wealth fairly
medium.explanation: The Lord can overturn human power by strengthening the spoiled against the strong.
medium.q: What does the phrase “strengtheneth the spoiled against the strong” describe?

answers: The Lord can overturn power and judge the oppressors
The Lord’s power is shown only through the stars
medium.explanation: The Lord rules creation and can bring judgment against those who abuse power.
medium.q: How are the Lord’s power and social injustice connected in this passage?

answers: The society rejects correction and honest speech
The people simply fail to understand the prophet
challenge.explanation: Their hatred shows that truth and correction are being rejected.
challenge.q: What can be inferred from the hatred of the reprover and the upright speaker?

answers: They show that unjust gains will not remain in the oppressors’ hands
They merely describe the beauty of the land
They command the people to plant vineyards
challenge.explanation: The passage connects exploiting the poor with losing the enjoyment of accumulated wealth.
challenge.q: Why are houses of hewn stone and pleasant vineyards mentioned alongside oppression?

answers: Conditions are so dangerous that even the discerning keep silent
The prudent leave town to find work
challenge.explanation: The prudent keep silence because the time is evil.
challenge.q: What does the silence of the prudent signify in the evil time?

paragraphs.title: The Way to Reform and the Coming Mourning

easy.explanation: The prophet says, “Seek good, and not evil.”
easy.q: What does the prophet tell the people to seek?

easy.explanation: They are told to establish judgment in the gate.
easy.q: What are the people told to establish in the gate?

easy.explanation: The passage mentions the possibility that the Lord may be gracious to the remnant of Joseph.
easy.q: On whom might the Lord be gracious?

answers: They are presented as a way that the people may live
They cause the people to go to war
medium.explanation: The people are told to seek good so that they may live.
medium.q: How are hating evil and loving good connected with life?

answers: Wailing will spread through the streets, highways, and vineyards
The people will return to the worship centers
medium.explanation: The prophet describes wailing in the streets, highways, and vineyards.
medium.q: What will happen if there is no reform?

medium.explanation: A remnant is what remains after a larger group has suffered loss.
medium.q: What does “remnant” mean in “the remnant of Joseph”?

answers: Mercy is presented as a hope, not as a guaranteed outcome
Mercy has no connection with repentance
challenge.explanation: The phrase expresses possibility and hope rather than certainty.
challenge.q: What does “it may be” show about the possibility of mercy?

answers: Moral reform may bring life and mercy, while failure brings mourning
The future is determined only by wealth
Human actions do not affect the future
challenge.explanation: The passage presents a relationship between conduct and its consequences.
challenge.q: How does the prophet connect the people’s actions with their future?

answers: To show that the disaster will reach throughout every part of life
To command the people to plant vineyards
challenge.explanation: Wailing in both public places and vineyards emphasizes the widespread nature of the disaster.
challenge.q: Why is mourning described in vineyards as well as in the city?

paragraphs.title: The Day of the Lord as Darkness and Judgment

easy.explanation: The passage repeatedly describes it as darkness and not light.
easy.q: How is the day of the Lord described?

easy.explanation: The man flees from a lion.
easy.q: What animal does the man flee from first?

easy.explanation: The KJV says, “and a bear met him.”
easy.q: What meets the man after he flees from the lion?

answers: He expects light, but the day will be darkness and judgment
He expects war, but the day will be commerce
He does not know the date of the day
medium.explanation: Amos warns that the day of the Lord will not be the expected day of light.
medium.q: Why is the person who desires the day of the Lord mistaken?

answers: There is no escape from the danger
Human beings are stronger than every animal
medium.explanation: Each attempt to escape leads to another danger.
medium.q: What does the example of the lion, bear, and serpent emphasize?

medium.explanation: The words intensify the image of complete darkness.
medium.q: What does “very dark, and no brightness” mean?

answers: Repetition of the contrast between darkness and light
challenge.explanation: The repeated contrast emphasizes that the day will be judgment rather than light.
challenge.q: What literary device is central to the description of the day of the Lord?

answers: Danger surrounds the person both outside and inside
Danger exists only on the road
challenge.explanation: The examples show that neither the open way nor the house provides safety.
challenge.q: What does the movement from the lion to the bear and from the house to the serpent suggest?

answers: Expectation of light gives way to the realization of unavoidable darkness
challenge.explanation: Amos overturns the expectation of a bright day and presents one of darkness.
challenge.q: How does the person’s expectation of the day of the Lord change?

paragraphs.title: Rejection of Worship Without Justice and Righteousness

answers: He does not know about them
easy.explanation: The Lord says, “I hate, I despise your feast days.”
easy.q: What does the Lord say about the people’s feast days?

answers: The offerings and songs when justice is absent
easy.explanation: The Lord rejects the sacrifices, offerings, assemblies, and songs described in the passage.
easy.q: What does the Lord refuse to accept?

easy.explanation: Judgment should run down as waters and righteousness as a mighty stream.
easy.q: What should judgment and righteousness be like?

answers: It is not accompanied by judgment and righteousness
The feast days are too short
medium.explanation: The passage demands justice and righteousness rather than empty ritual.
medium.q: Why does the Lord reject the people’s worship?

medium.explanation: The phrase refers to animals chosen for sacrifice.
medium.q: What are “fat beasts” in the context of the offerings?

answers: Justice and righteousness should be visible and continual
medium.explanation: Flowing water represents an ongoing and evident practice of justice.
medium.q: What does the image of waters and a mighty stream express?

answers: Worship without social justice is not acceptable to the Lord
Ritual is more important than moral action
challenge.explanation: The Lord rejects worship that is separated from judgment and righteousness.
challenge.q: What principle does this passage establish about worship?

answers: It contrasts ritual noise with active, continual moral conduct
It describes a change in the weather
challenge.explanation: The passage turns attention from songs to the living practice of justice.
challenge.q: How does the contrast between loud songs and flowing waters strengthen the message?

answers: Justice should spread openly and broadly rather than remain hidden
Justice should occur only beside rivers
challenge.explanation: The image of flowing water suggests reach, visibility, and continuity.
challenge.q: What is implied by the command for judgment to run like waters?

paragraphs.title: Sacrifices and Idols Cannot Prevent Exile

easy.explanation: The passage asks about sacrifices offered in the wilderness forty years.
easy.q: How many years in the wilderness are mentioned?

answers: The tabernacle of Moloch and the images of Chiun
Only the ark of the covenant
easy.explanation: The passage names the tabernacle of Moloch and Chiun, their images.
easy.q: What did the people carry along with their images?

easy.explanation: The Lord says he will cause them to go into captivity beyond Damascus.
easy.q: Where would the Lord cause the people to go into captivity?

answers: Reliance on sacrifices as a substitute for correcting injustice
medium.explanation: The question challenges the idea that ritual offerings can replace moral obedience.
medium.q: What does Amos challenge by asking about sacrifices in the wilderness?

answers: Idols or figures made by human hands
medium.explanation: Images here refer to idols or representations made by the people.
medium.q: What are “images” in the phrase “Chiun your images”?

answers: The idols cannot save the people, who go into exile with them
The idols protect the people on their journey
The people leave the idols behind in the land
medium.explanation: The passage portrays the people carrying their powerless idols into captivity.
medium.q: What is the connection between carrying the idols and going into captivity?

answers: Neither ritual nor idols can prevent judgment
The idols complete and improve the sacrifices
Sacrifices remove the need for righteousness
challenge.explanation: The passage rejects trust in both outward ritual and false gods as protection from judgment.
challenge.q: What is the significance of the movement from sacrifices to idols at the end of the passage?

answers: Exile results from a society that has not corrected its wrongs through outward worship
Exile is presented as a reward for righteousness
The ending has no connection with the earlier message
challenge.explanation: The chapter teaches that external worship cannot prevent judgment when injustice remains.
challenge.q: How does the ending connect with the earlier theme of justice?

answers: The exile will take the people far from their land
The people will immediately return to Bethel
The people will remain in the wilderness
challenge.explanation: “Beyond Damascus” emphasizes the distance and severity of the exile.
challenge.q: What does the mention of Damascus emphasize?
